name: Million Qubit Requirement
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Why a Few Thousand Qubits Isn't the Finish Line
lesson.summary: Multiplying the number of logical qubits a real algorithm needs by the thousand-to-one error-correction overhead lands squarely in the millions of physical qubits, which is why that figure keeps showing up as the field's real target.
lesson.body:
Once the thousand-to-one physical-to-logical ratio is on the table, the natural next question is how many logical qubits an actually useful algorithm needs, because multiplying those two numbers together is what tells you the true size of machine required. For breaking a 2048-bit RSA key with Shor's algorithm, one of the most carefully studied resource estimates, published in 2019 by Craig Gidney and Martin Ekera, concluded that the task would need on the order of 20 million physical qubits running for about eight hours, given realistic assumptions about physical error rates and surface-code overhead. Quantum chemistry simulations aimed at industrially relevant molecules, and optimization problems at a genuinely competitive scale, land in similar territory: thousands of logical qubits translating into millions of physical qubits once error correction and magic-state distillation are included.

This is why the million-qubit requirement has become a common shorthand in the field for the scale at which quantum computers start solving problems that are actually hard for classical computers, using algorithms we already know how to write, reliably enough that errors do not swamp the answer. It is not a marketing target picked for round-number appeal. It falls out of multiplying a real algorithm's logical qubit count by a real error-correction code's physical overhead.

The gap between that target and what has been built is enormous. As of the mid-2020s, the largest quantum processors built by any group, across superconducting, trapped-ion, and neutral-atom platforms, held physical qubit counts in the hundreds to low thousands, not millions. That is not a small shortfall to close with a few more years of incremental improvement. It is roughly three orders of magnitude, and every one of those orders of magnitude runs into the physical constraints covered elsewhere in this chapter: how the qubits are wired, how they are cooled, how much power the system draws, and how much the whole apparatus costs.

It is worth being precise about what this requirement does and does not say. It does not say a million-qubit quantum computer is impossible. It says that today's architectures, scaled up by brute-force replication of current designs, run into serious engineering obstacles long before they reach that scale, which is why so much current research effort goes into finding better error-correcting codes, better qubit designs, and modular architectures that might lower the multiplier rather than simply building bigger versions of what exists now.

It is also worth noting that estimates like the 20 million qubit figure keep shifting, and generally downward, as researchers find more efficient ways to compile algorithms, better magic-state distillation schemes, and codes with lower overhead than the plain surface code. That downward trend is genuine progress. But even generous improvements of several times over still leave the target in the millions, not the thousands, which is why the million-qubit requirement remains a useful anchor for how far current hardware still has to travel before it can run the algorithms that would matter most.
